newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New Chernogorneft P&L said affected by inflation.
newsitem.headline: New Chernogorneft P&L said affected by inflation.

text.p: International-standard accounts from Russian oil producer Chernogorneft showed sharply higher profits than Russian-standard audits, but analysts on Friday said inflationary factors had swollen the profits.

AOOT Chernogorneft, the main production unit of NK SIDANKO, showed 1995 net profit of 582 billion roubles, after 807 billion, adjusted for inflation in 1994, an audit by Ernst & Young according to U.S. GAAP shows.
Net income in the first half of 1995 to Russian standards on a cash basis was only 66.6 billion roubles.

But the net profit in the U.S. GAAP statement included hefty gains on holding net monetary liabilities, essentially gains made when payments were delayed and hyperinflation reduced the real value of the liabilities.
"If you are able to delay the payment of any liability in fixed terms in a hyperinflationary economy you have reduced those costs and made a gain," said Chuck Buckner, audit partner at Ernst & Young.

Chernogorneft gains from this kind of payment delay were 456 billion roubles in 1995 and 1.1 trillion roubles, adjusted for inflation, in 1994, on sales of 2.5 trillion roubles and 2.2 trillion roubles, respectively.
As a result Chernogorneft's net income and income before tax were much bigger than its operating profit.
Chernogorneft's financial advisor SovLink said the new statement showed the company was stronger than Russian accounting suggested.
"Even if you discount the holding sum, you will find its earnings are a lot stronger than under Russian financials," said Michael Boboshko, a Sovlink analyst.
But other analysts said the new statement indicated oil companies could face increasing financial problems from taxes without the inflationary buffer.

"They were trying to collect as soon as possible and pay as late as possible," said CentreInvest Securities research chief James Fenkner. "If inflation comes down, taxation will have to come down, or Chernogorneft could face a loss," he said.
Government exactions, including VAT, excise and other non-profits taxes were 841 billion roubles in 1995 and 964 billion roubles in 1994. Income taxes were 137 billion in 1995 and 63 billion in 1994.
Gavin Rankin, head of research at Troika-Dialog, said the gains should be stripped out when analysing the company.

"I'm not going to revalue Chernogorneft on these figures," he said, adding that taking out the inflation gains gave roughly the same picture as the Russian-standard books. "It's what we expected," he said.
Western analysts said delayed payments was one of the few ways to survive such a high tax environment, where oil company taxes are about 55 percent of sales.
"This is a good healthy company. But taxes are at the level where hardly anybody can operate. If you hold the liability just over the year, you reduce the costs," said one analyst.

Economists gave Chernogorneft high marks for publishing the new figures, which show operating profit in 1995 of 108 billion roubles and an operating loss of 160 billion roubles in 1994. By Russian cash-based accounting, 1995 first-half operating profit was 150 billion roubles.
Fenkner said the huge inflationary distortion could be the same for the rest of the industry.
"Just because they are the first out, does not mean this is not the case with Surgutneftegaz or Yuganskneftegaz," he said. "This may be the shape of things to come."
